extracted.intended_audience: poets, students of poetics, translators, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on composing poetic diction (metaphors, epithets, invented/altered words) drawn from Aristotle and commentary; covers when devices elevate or degrade poetry and how they should be used by poets and translators. Focuses on clarity vs loftiness and matching devices to genre/meter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer analogical metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: "we should always endeavour to chuse the Analogical one, because 'tis the finest, and most esteemed" — an analogical metaphor consists not only in resemblance but in an entire proportion or relation between terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogical metaphors are the finest type and should be preferred. They rest on a proportional relation across pairs of terms (e.g., Life:Old Age :: Day:Evening). Use analogical metaphors to achieve the highest poetic effect; they carry both likeness and a systematic relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for a proper analogical metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Every metaphor grounded on analogy "must necessarily have these two Conditions: First, That it may be inverted, and that the Terms when transposed, equally answer one to another. Secondly, That 'tis grounded on things of the same Nature and Kind."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify invertibility (terms can be transposed and still correspond) and that the paired subjects are of the same nature/kind. Examples: Life/Old Age/Day/Evening; Mars/Shield :: Bacchus/Cup. If both conditions hold, the metaphor will be stable and highly esteemed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid (or treat cautiously) imperfect/one-way analogies
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes a term is borrowed for one subject but there is no reciprocal term for the other (e.g., we say the Sun 'sows' light borrowing from husbandman's 'sow', but you cannot borrow a term back). The analogy is then imperfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when a metaphor is one-way: it may be useful but is less perfect than a fully reciprocal analogy. Such metaphors can be effective (ancients used them), but they lack the symmetry and philosophical neatness of true analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitute by the thing to which the resemblance is made
rubrics_metrics.description: Often the thing to which the resemblance is made is added and put instead of that from which the resemblance is taken (e.g., instead of saying 'a Cup is a Shield' one says 'the Shield of Bacchus' or 'the Cup of Mars').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the target of resemblance as the referring term is a common and acceptable poetic device (metonymic/metaphorical substitution). It is a conventional practice illustrated by many ancient examples; use it to create compact, resonant phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative-epithet metaphors (the 'without X')
rubrics_metrics.description: A manner of using metaphor where, in lieu of the subject's name, a negative epithet is added which denies some quality proper to the metaphorical term (e.g., 'a Bow is a Harp without strings', 'an harmony without lute').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative-epithet constructions are valued in analogy-based metaphors and used frequently in Greek poetry. They can be striking and elegant, but their intelligibility depends on cultural/linguistic context; use them where the denial sharpens contrast or heightens effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of epithets (ornament) but with limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Epithets are ornaments that 'the Poets use at every turn to grace and adorn their Discourses', yet 'if a Poem is too full of Epithets 'tis flat; if they are ill chosen, and not well adapted, 'tis ridiculous and displeasing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ epithets to enrich and identify, but avoid overuse. Choose epithets adapted to context and character; badly chosen or excessive epithets produce ridicule (example: Cleophon). Epithets should ornament, not overwhelm, the diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invented names (neologisms) are permissible for poets
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'Invented Name' is one the poet himself creates (Aristotle notes Homer invented several); these are typically simple words rather than compound forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neologisms can add novelty and poetic identity; classical precedent (Homer) shows value. Use inventively but sparingly — and consider intelligibility and tradition in your language, since some languages (like Latin/English) lack the Greek freedom for such invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protracted, subtracted, and altered words as stylistic resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Protracted nouns (long vowel for short), subtracted nouns (syllable removed), and other letter changes were used in Greek for variety and musicality. These changes confer extraordinary quality while retaining some recognizability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morphological alteration can lend loftiness and novelty while preserving enough of the proper word to keep clarity. Use these transformations judiciously — they are more native to Greek; in other languages be mindful of naturalness and intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance purity (clarity) and nobleness (loftiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The virtue of an expression consists in its Purity and Nobleness: 'that which is composed of simple words is very clear; but 'tis also low... to render it at the same time clear and noble, make use of protracted, subtracted, and changed words.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a mixture: proper/simple words give clarity, borrowed/figurative/altered words give loftiness. The optimal diction preserves intelligibility while achieving elevation. Excess on either side produces plainness or obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation from continual use of ornaments
rubrics_metrics.description: Affectation arises not from the devices themselves but from their continual use: 'tis not the thing itself which makes the Affectation, 'tis the continual using these manners of Speech.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not habitually saturate diction with the same ornamental techniques; occasional, well-placed devices are effective, continuous deployment appears forced and ridiculous. Monitor frequency and apparent intent — deliberate showiness is a flaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figured speech must be agreeable, well placed, and in just proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: To evidence the beauty of figured speech, 'provided they be agreeable, well placed, and in just Proportion', otherwise substituting figurative words for proper ones may not advance the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess placement and proportionality of figurative language within line, stanza, and whole work. A striking metaphor in a wrong place or too many consecutive ornate phrases will spoil rather than improve; ensure each figure serves a purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign words give loftiness but risk barbarism if overused
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign words 'give a Loftiness and Majesty to the Discourse, when they are used with Moderation and Discretion, but make it Barbarous, when they are used too often.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use loanwords selectively to add grandeur or exotic color; excessive foreign lexis produces obscurity or a barbarous effect. Consider audience familiarity and the tradition of the language when introducing foreign terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match rhetorical devices to meter/genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Different devices suit different verse types: 'The double Words agree particularly to Dithyrambicks. The Foreign Words to Heroick, and the Metaphors to Iambick Verses...the iambick, which imitates only the Familiar Style, can employ no Terms but such as are used in Conversation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose devices that fit the genre and meter: heroic verse tolerates foreign/archaic words; dithyrambic verse favors doubling; iambic (conversational) prefers proper, familiar words. Align diction with the expectations of the form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for a proper riddle
rubrics_metrics.description: A true enigma or riddle requires (a) the use of a metaphor, (b) that the proposition makes the thing appear impossible, and (c) the subject of it be natural and known to everybody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting riddles, ensure they are metaphorical, produce apparent impossibility, and refer to commonly-known subjects; failure of any condition weakens the riddle (example: Samson's riddle lacks universality). Classical examples ("I saw a man who glued tin to a man with fire") show successful application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figurative devices enhance only when they express the right effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing proper words by metaphors or foreign words does not automatically improve expression; the device must express the intended quality (e.g., 'The Rivers roar' is better than 'The Rivers cried' to render a terrible sea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select figurative or remote expressions that match the desired sensory/emotional effect. Test substitutions — if a figurative term heightens the intended impression (terror, grandeur, pathos), it's justified; if not, prefer the proper term.
